problems.stem: A classroom implementation plan for an AI math-practice tool lists the lesson activities and the login steps. A mentor says it is not yet a defensible plan. What is most clearly missing?
options: A longer description of the tool's features.
A rollout that names what happens when the tool fails or a student cannot access it, plus who is responsible at each step.
More screenshots of the tool interface.
A statement that the tool is popular with other teachers.
problems.explanation: An implementation plan must anticipate failure modes, access gaps, and responsibility, not just describe the happy-path activity.

problems.stem: A reviewer annotates a plan: "You scheduled the AI tool for week 1, but the parental-consent forms are not collected until week 3." What kind of error does this expose?
options: A formatting error in the timeline table.
A sequencing error: a required consent gate is scheduled after the activity that depends on it, so the plan is not yet enactable.
A word-choice problem in the activity description.
A missing citation for the consent policy.
problems.explanation: An enactable plan orders dependencies correctly; a consent gate must clear before the activity it protects.

problems.stem: A teacher asks BigAL to generate a week-by-week rollout schedule for the new tool. What is the defensible boundary on using that draft?
options: Adopt the schedule as written, since the model balanced the weeks for you.
Use the draft as a checklist, then adjust it against the real school calendar, device-cart availability, and consent timeline the model could not know.
Ask the model to also pick which students get the tool first.
Trust the schedule because it cites instructional-design principles.
problems.explanation: AI can produce a generic schedule, but the teacher must reconcile it with local constraints the model cannot see.

problems.stem: Two implementation plans target the same AI tool. Plan A defines success as "all students complete the module." Plan B defines success as "the median student gains at least one proficiency level and no subgroup falls further behind." Why is Plan B more defensible?
options: Plan B is longer and uses more measurement language.
Plan B ties the tool to a learning outcome and an equity guardrail, so the plan can be evaluated and stopped if it harms a subgroup.
Plan A is wrong because completion never matters.
Plan B will guarantee better results in any classroom.
problems.explanation: A defensible plan defines success as a learning outcome with an equity check, making the rollout evaluable and stoppable.
